canDo: Can recognise the three question types that cost the most marks in B2 reading and listening (implied meaning, author’s tone/position, paraphrase) and give answers backed by the text using a three-step method: “locate the passage → find the paraphrase → eliminate distractors”.
review: Review your wrong answers in reading and listening from Mock 1 and Mock 2: which were “didn’t hear it / didn’t find it”, which were misunderstandings and which were caused by distractors; go back over the markers of concession, irony and reservation (certes, pourtant, je ne prétends pas que, sans tomber dans).
input: Read: a long article on functional illiteracy in adults, an ironic column “in defence of boredom” and a restaurant owner’s reply to a bad review; write down the evidence in the text for each question. Listen: a debate on “parking charges based on vehicle weight”, a linguist on English loanwords at work and a pollen alert news flash; on the first listen focus only on structure and positions, on the second check details and paraphrases.
output: Write: an article for a community newspaper on adults’ reading and writing difficulties (250+ words), with a headline, a description of the situation, an analysis of the consequences and concrete proposals; speak: a 5-minute monologue on “should daylight saving time be abolished?”, then a debate with the examiner on “parking charges based on vehicle weight”.
checkpoint: Reading + listening accuracy ≥85%, with every tone/implied-meaning question correct; for each question, can say in one sentence of your own language where the evidence is and why the distractors are wrong; can summarise both sides’ arguments in L44-1 and one concession.
challenge: Today’s challenge: find a debate or interview with two points of view on TV5MONDE or RFI (3 minutes or less), listen only once, then write in French “A pense que… / B réplique que… / Les deux s’accordent sur…”; check against the transcript and count the paraphrases you missed.

questions.why: The article defines illettrisme, then explains how hidden it is (paragraph 2), its effects (paragraph 3), remedies and obstacles (paragraph 4), and ends by calling for a change of attitude (« que l’on peut surmonter à tout âge »). B: the text doesn’t discuss primary school teaching; C: the author attributes it to shame and doesn’t criticise those affected.
« Ces personnes ont pourtant été scolarisées… à ne pas confondre avec l’analphabétisme, qui concerne ceux qui n’ont jamais appris à lire ». A has no basis; C contradicts « la lecture et l’écriture ».

« d’autant plus difficile à mesurer qu’il se cache », followed by a list of cover-up strategies (claiming to have forgotten their glasses, asking relatives to fill in forms, etc.). Neither A nor B is mentioned.

The first half, « Ils ne sont pas moins intelligents que les autres », shows that all their intelligence goes into hiding the problem. A takes it literally; C: the text talks about “hiding”, not “teaching themselves”.
« là où l’on pouvait autrefois se faire aider au guichet, il faut désormais lire et écrire seul devant un écran ». Neither B nor C is in the text.

« Tant que l’illettrisme sera perçu comme un échec individuel… ceux qui en souffrent continueront de se taire »: society’s view must change first before those affected dare to speak up. A is exactly the view the author criticises; B contradicts the praise for workshops in paragraph 4.

« Pauvre ennui ! », « un seau percé » and « sans doute plus fort » are humorous and exaggerated, but paragraph 3 makes a serious point drawing on psychology. A: the tone isn’t alarmed; C: the author takes a clear position.
Pouring water into a leaky bucket never fills it: endless scrolling never fills the empty time either; it’s futile. B is a literal misreading; C is irrelevant.

Before this: « Je ne prétends pas qu’ils étaient plus heureux »: the author heads off any “nostalgia filter” and only stresses that they were able to be “bored”. A is exactly the conclusion he rejects; B: he isn’t criticising anyone.
« l’esprit vagabonde, établit des liens inattendus, invente… les meilleures idées ». Neither B nor C is in the text.
« très sérieusement » is self-mocking, but the suggestion fits the text’s argument (idle time sparks creativity). A is the author’s idea, not reality; C ties in with the logic of the whole text.
It is the owner’s public reply to a one-star review (« Réponse du propriétaire »). Neither B nor C is in the text.

The bad review was posted at 20:12, but the main course only arrived at 20:15: the customer wrote the review before finishing the meal, and the owner uses this to imply it was hasty. A and C draw the wrong conclusions from the numbers.
« Nous aurions sans doute dû vous en informer dès votre arrivée ; c’est une erreur ». B: he defends the waiter; A isn’t covered.

Polite on the surface (« Merci », « Nous serions heureux »), but « Nous sommes toujours ravis… surtout lorsqu’ils sont rédigés à chaud » is clearly ironic. B: there is no insulting language; C: his reply is very detailed.

The host opens with « Faut-il faire payer plus cher le stationnement aux voitures les plus lourdes ? ». B isn’t mentioned; C is too broad: the measure only concerns parking charges, and residents aren’t affected.

« Ces voitures prennent plus de place, abîment davantage la chaussée et… elles sont plus dangereuses pour les piétons et les cyclistes ». A isn’t mentioned; C: although it only targets visitors from outside, she doesn’t give that as a reason.

« Pensez aux familles nombreuses, aux artisans, aux personnes handicapées… cette mesure est une punition ». He explicitly denies A; B: he only says “weight doesn’t tell the whole story”, not that heavy cars pollute less.
« Nous avons étudié les véhicules concernés… ceux-là bénéficient d’ailleurs d’une exemption ». B and C are the opposite of her position.

« on n’a pas vraiment consulté les automobilistes… C’est surtout ça que je reproche à la mairie » (a cleft sentence). A: what he doubts is the aim of “raising revenue”, not overspending; C isn’t criticised.
« je reconnais que la concertation aurait pu être meilleure ». A and B: she sticks to her views throughout.

The host’s question and her answer are both about English loanwords at work (« Faire un call », « envoyer un mail »). B isn’t covered; C: she only mentions in passing that languages borrow from each other.
« c’est une question d’image : on a l’impression que l’anglais fait plus moderne, plus international ». A contradicts « quand un mot français existe »; C isn’t mentioned.
« ne comprend pas tout, mais n’ose pas le dire… à la longue, certains finissent par se taire et par se sentir à l’écart ». A and B are exaggerated or not mentioned.
« apprenez les deux… il faut les comprendre. Mais à l’écrit… préférez le mot français ». A is too absolute; C is exactly the attitude she criticises.
« jusqu’à dimanche au moins ». Neither B nor C is mentioned.
« les écoles sont invitées à limiter les activités sportives en extérieur ». A isn’t mentioned; C is the opposite of the advice to air rooms only early in the morning or in the evening.
« peuvent recevoir chaque matin, par SMS, le niveau de risque de leur commune en s’inscrivant »; chaque matin paraphrases chaque jour. Neither A nor B is mentioned.

V44-01.zh: (two things) to go hand in hand
V44-01.exZh: In big cities, air pollution and traffic noise go hand in hand.

V44-02.zh: to take a toll on health
V44-02.exZh: Lack of sleep eventually takes a toll on health.

V44-03.zh: in its own right, fully fledged
V44-03.exZh: Functional illiteracy should be seen as a difficulty in its own right.

V44-04.zh: to walk through the door of; (figuratively) to pluck up the courage to go somewhere
V44-04.exZh: Many adults don’t dare walk through the door of a literacy workshop.

V44-05.zh: the poor relation, the forgotten one
V44-05.exZh: In this budget, culture remains the poor relation.

V44-06.zh: to take the side of, to stand up for
V44-06.exZh: In his column, the author stands up for boredom.

V44-07.zh: a leaky bucket; (figuratively) a bottomless pit
V44-07.exZh: Filling every minute is like pouring water into a leaky bucket.

V44-08.zh: (emotions) to be a bad counsellor, not to be trusted
V44-08.exZh: Don’t decide anything tonight: anger is a bad counsellor.

V44-09.zh: a gap, downtime (time with nothing to do)
V44-09.exZh: He uses every gap to revise his vocabulary.

V44-10.exZh: During the meeting, his mind began to wander.

V44-11.exZh: I love wandering aimlessly through the alleys of the old town.

V44-12.zh: to be swamped, rushed off one’s feet
V44-12.exZh: That evening, the waiter was swamped with orders.

V44-13.exZh: Heavy vehicles damage the road surface faster than others.

V44-14.exZh: Heavy cars take up more public space than other vehicles.

V44-15.zh: not to tell the whole story
V44-15.exZh: A car’s weight doesn’t tell the whole story about how much it pollutes.

V44-16.exZh: Vehicles adapted for disabled people are exempt.

V44-17.zh: to fill the coffers (of a government, an institution)
V44-17.exZh: Is this charge just a way to fill the town hall’s coffers?

V44-18.zh: let’s grant that, even supposing so
V44-18.exZh: Let’s grant that the measure is useful: who will bear the cost?

V44-19.exZh: The idea that girls are less gifted at maths is a stubborn prejudice.

V44-20.zh: in the long run, over time
V44-20.exZh: These little remarks wear you down over time.

V44-21.exZh: In pollen season, it’s best to air your home early in the morning.

V44-22.exZh: Without help, it’s hard to cope with online procedures on your own.

V44-23.zh: a (regular) drop-in service, a help desk
V44-23.exZh: The town could open a drop-in service to help people fill in forms.

V44-24.zh: to be at a standstill, to stall
V44-24.exZh: The EU plan to abolish daylight saving time has stalled.

V44-25.exZh: For some, the clock change is a non-issue.
